questionText: Explain Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) with definition, comparison against 3NF, and decomposition algorithm with example.
studentAnswer:
Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) is a stricter version of Third Normal Form (3NF). A relational schema R is in BCNF if for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey of R. In contrast, 3NF relaxes this condition by allowing Y to be a prime attribute (part of any candidate key) even if X is not a superkey. Therefore, every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but not every 3NF relation is in BCNF.

Consider relation R(A, B, C) with functional dependencies: AB -> C and C -> B. Here, Candidate Keys are AB and AC. For dependency C -> B, C is not a superkey, but B is a prime attribute (part of candidate key AB). Hence, R is in 3NF but violates BCNF. To decompose R into BCNF, we split R into R1(C, B) with key C, and R2(A, C) with key AC. The decomposition is lossless because R1 intersect R2 = {C}, which is a superkey of R1. However, dependency AB -> C cannot be preserved without computing natural join.

questionText: Explain Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) with definition, comparison against 3NF, and decomposition algorithm with example.
studentAnswer: BCNF stands for Boyce Codd Normal Form. It was created by Raymond Boyce and Edgar Codd. It removes anomalies from database tables. A relation is in BCNF if for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey of the table. It is higher than 1NF and 2NF. In 3NF there can be redundancy due to candidate keys overlapping. In BCNF that is not allowed.

questionText: Explain Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) with definition, comparison against 3NF, and decomposition algorithm with example.
studentAnswer: BCNF is weaker than 3NF. In BCNF any attribute can depend on non-prime attributes without restrictions. 3NF is the highest normal form and every relation in 3NF is automatically in BCNF. To convert to BCNF we simply remove multi-valued attributes as in 1NF.
